# R18.7 — KAIYUANSHE COSR 2023–2025: Commercialization + Questionnaire chapters

Source: KAIYUANSHE, *China Open Source Annual Report* 2023, 2024 and 2025, English "Commercialization" and "Questionnaire" chapters (CC BY-SA 4.0). All six files were read in full. Claims are in `18.7-commercial-claims.tsv` (212 rows: 87 vc, 59 survey, 25 other, 18 business_model, 6 foundation, 5 revenue, 4 gov_fund, 4 m&a, 4 ipo). A script checked that every quote appears verbatim in the source and is 25 words or fewer.

## What kind of source this is (read first)
- **2023 chapter**: written by the investment team of **Yunqi Partners**, a VC that names its own portfolio (PingCAP, Zilliz, Jina AI, RisingWave, TabbyML, Realchar). It contains the only deal-level data in the three years: Table 4.1 (58 Chinese OSS startups) and Table 4.2 (9 open-weight LLM startups). Evidence level: **C/B**. It is secondary, and it comes from a party with an interest in the outcome.
- **2024 chapter**: opinion interviews with four RMB/USD investors (Guofang Innovation, Delian Capital, INP, Atypical Ventures). It gives **no deal amounts**. Use it for qualitative claims only (**C**).
- **2025 chapter**: synthesis by KAIYUANSHE. It reuses the 2025 Data Report (OpenRank) and Linux Foundation, CNCF and Serena/COSSA reports. It gives **no Chinese company financing figures**. Its global VC and exit numbers are Western sources cited at second hand. Cite the original LF reports instead (**B** via citation).
- **Translation problems in Table 4.1**: company names are machine translations, e.g. "Tributary Technologies" for 支流科技 (API7.ai) and "Fly to Cloud" for 飞致云 (FIT2CLOUD). The TSV marks our identifications as "likely". Amount cells read "dollars" where the original was almost certainly 元. For example, "Tianmou Technology (IoTDB) angel round — nearly a billion dollars" is implausible and is probably 近亿元 (about CNY 100M). The TSV currency column says "USD as translated (may be CNY)". **Do not convert these amounts to EUR without checking the Chinese 2023 edition.** Three dates are Excel serials (44958, 44986, 45108 → Feb, Mar and Jul 2023). We converted them and flagged each one.

## 10 key findings for the funding comparison (new vs PROJECT-FUNDING.md / FUNDING-COMPARISON.md)
1. **A VC funding layer we have not recorded (new).** Table 4.1 lists 58 Chinese OSS companies with their latest round. Most rounds are angel to B, and amounts run from "millions" to ~1bn CNY. Five companies behind projects already in PROJECT-FUNDING.md have rows here: API7 (APISIX, A+, 2021-06), VeloDB/SelectDB (Doris; Pre-A 2023-06, cumulative "nearly 1 billion yuan"), PingCAP (TiDB, round E 2021-07, amount undisclosed), Zilliz (Milvus; B+ US$60M 2022-08, and in the text a US$43M Series B) and Dify (2023-03, undisclosed). This turns the "VC" label on TiDB, Dify and Doris from inference into a sourced (C) round list. Those rows could feed a new instrument type `equity-vc` (CN) in data/funding.
2. **Explicit RMB amounts for open-weight LLM startups (Table 4.2).** Zhipu AI raised 12 亿人民币 (CNY 1.2bn, 2023-09-19). Baichuan raised 3 亿美元 (US$300M, 2023-10-17). XVERSE raised 1.2 亿美元 (2022-03). DP Technology raised 超 7 亿人民币 (2023-08). Mainland Chinese open-model work is mostly VC-funded. DeepSeek is the exception: it is funded by High-Flyer (already in our data).
3. **Gitee/OSChina's B+ round of CNY 775M (2023-07)** is the largest single OSS-infrastructure round in the corpus. Gitee is the state-backed national code platform, so this is relevant to our "public money" framing. The report gives no investors. We have not verified the Chinese-language press reports that say state funds took part.
4. **The USD-to-RMB shift (2024).** Investors report that the "legislation from early this year" (the US outbound investment rules) "had a severe impact on USD investments". Funding is moving to RMB funds "with increasing support from local governments". The 2023 KPMG data quoted in the chapter shows the same trend: foreign-currency funds fell 67% in H1 2023 to US$24.7bn, while RMB funds rose 13%. Inference for us: Chinese COSS equity is becoming state-guided RMB capital. That blurs our boundary between public and private money.
5. **Where Chinese buyers' money comes from.** Software revenue is an "inverted pyramid", with most of it from SOEs and central-government enterprises (2024). The home-market models are listed as "government and enterprise procurement… domestic substitution, private deployment" (2025). This supports our finding #7 (Xinchuang procurement as China's version of government-as-customer). It also gives a second-hand quote we can cite.
6. **Investors see weak willingness to pay and a broken commercial loop.** iResearch (2023) finds firms are "more willing to pay for manpower" than for software. Investors in 2024 report weak copyright compliance, budget rules that favour hardware that can be capitalised, cancelled OSS investment mandates, and the view that in China open source "has little to do with commercialization". This helps explain our finding #3 (almost no donation channel). The only overseas monetisation benchmark given: PingCAP, StarRocks and EMQ each have "multiple overseas customers" paying millions of USD a year.
7. **Survey: individual funding is minimal.** In 2023, more than half of contributors received no financial reward, and donations or ad income were "very few". In 2024, nearly 40% received no direct return. In 2025, salary came first and "no return" second, and donations, advertising and service revenue were each single-digit shares. This is the developer-side counterpart of our Open Collective finding (Ant Design ~US$18k, KubeSphere US$0).
8. **Survey: corporate support of communities.** In 2024, among operators, co-development was 10.2%, formal adoption 8.7%, "resources or financial sponsorship" 8.4% and none 4.8%. These are multi-select shares, so they cannot be summed. In 2025, sponsorship with resources or funding was cited by "more than half". Funding is a minor perceived success factor: 16.8% in 2024. All of this is self-reported by operators (D for magnitudes).
9. **The governance model behind the OpenAtom projects is stated directly (2025).** The report calls for "a foundation serving as a public foundation, with commercial distribution vendors providing trusted delivery". It frames Huawei's model as resting on "the demand for self-reliance". This supports our OpenHarmony/openEuler channel stack (finding #1). The report gives no OpenAtom money figures, so CN-FOUNDATIONS.md remains our source.
10. **Local and public funding appears only in passing.** The report mentions a Shanghai OSS industry plan being drafted (Nov 2023) and Pudong Software Park bringing in the Linux Foundation Asia-Pacific service centre. It mentions "open-source industrial parks and innovation funds" in Haidian and Changping (Beijing, 2025). It gives **no amounts**. Nothing here adds to the caps in FUNDING-COMPARISON §1c. Treat these as leads for searches of the Shanghai, Haidian and Changping portals.

Also worth citing, but not about China. The global COSS figures in the 2025 chapter (LF Research, Serena, COSSA): US$26.4bn across 211 deals in 2024, 5% of software VC; median IPO valuation US$1.3bn vs US$171M for closed source; median M&A US$482M vs US$34M. The LF ROI survey: foundation contributions return 4.8x, direct financial contributions 2.4x. **Serena is a Paris-based VC**, which gives us a European-authored source for the comparison. Take it from the LF PDF rather than from KAIYUANSHE.

## Survey methodology and limits
| | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| n | 875 | 631 | 350 |
| Questions | 43 | 41 | 37 |
| Mode | online questionnaire | online + offline | online + offline |
| Channels | KAIYUANSHE; KubeCon/OSS Summit China; COSCon 2023; OpenAtom Developers Conf.; Open Source Industry Ecology Conf. | KAIYUANSHE official accounts; OSCAR conf.; PyCon; COSCon 2024 | KAIYUANSHE channels; CSDN WeChat reposts; COSCon'25 |
| Sampling | **opt-in convenience sample**, no weighting, no response rate | same | same |

Limits:
- All three samples are self-selected respondents reached through KAIYUANSHE and event channels. The report admits the regional skew comes from where the survey was collected (2023: Jiangsu, Sichuan, Shanghai; 2024: Beijing, Guangdong, Shanghai; 2025: "tied to… offline events"). Results cannot be generalised to Chinese developers. Use them as evidence level **D**, and only as qualitative direction.
- The sample is shrinking (875 → 631 → 350), and its make-up changes: students are 43.2% in 2023, 36.3% in 2024, and in 2025 back-end and full-stack developers are about two-thirds. Year-on-year comparisons are therefore unreliable.
- **Internal inconsistencies:**
  - 2024 preview says "balanced gender ratio… each half", but the body says 71.0% male.
  - 2024 industry share (72.23%) is identical to 2023's, which suggests a copy-over.
  - 2025 preview says GitHub is the most used contribution platform, but the body has Gitee ~60%, AtomGit ~50% and GitHub ~30%.
  - 2025 mostly gives approximate shares ("close to half") instead of percentages.
  - Most charts exist only as images, so many percentages cannot be extracted from the text.
- **Topics the brief asked about but the surveys do not cover:** no question on employer *support* for contributing (only "salary" as a source of financial return), no question on foundation membership or participation, no question on funding sources for projects, no question on international participation beyond tools and platforms used, and **no question on Europe or overseas**. Licence awareness is covered (Apache, then MIT, in 2023–24; MIT ~60% in 2025; Mulan 10–20% in 2025). Contribution motives are covered (interest and community first; financial reward low).

## Anything about Europe
Europe is barely present in these chapters:
- **2024, Liu Chao (Atypical Ventures)** advises Chinese infrastructure firms to target "markets that European and American companies are reluctant to touch or tend to overlook, such as Japan, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia". Europe appears as a competitor, not as a market or a partner.
- **2024, Liu Jingyuan** says "compared to Western countries, copyright awareness in China is relatively weak". **2024, Ding Ning** says Chinese firms "encounter discrimination when expanding overseas", and that real open-source commercialisation happens in "developed countries with high per capita GDP".
- **2025**: Germany supplies 6.84% of contributions to US-led projects (China 7.81%), and Germany has 10 of the global top-100 OpenRank regions (China 8). The "Vibe Coding Kills Open Source" paper is by researchers at the Central European University and the Kiel Institute (the report says "University of Central Europe"). The proposed Compliance-as-a-Service model lists **GDPR** among the requirements to build into products. A Valkey-style neutral foundation and clear answers on governance ("Who owns the trademark?") are presented as preconditions for selling to overseas, including European, critical-infrastructure buyers.
- **2023**: one sentence on European AI funding (Poolside, which is French), and a note that ChatGPT-era licences restrict Chinese-language use. Nothing on EU funding programmes, the CRA, NGI/STF or EU–China cooperation.
- None of the three surveys asks about Europe.

## Suggested follow-ups
- Check Table 4.1 and 4.2 amounts and currencies against the Chinese 2023 edition (`kaiyuanshe/2023-China-Open-Source-Report`, zh). Only then add them to data/funding as a `cn` equity-vc layer (summable=false; private, not public).
- Look for the investors in Gitee's CNY 775M round, to check whether state funds took part.
- Search the Shanghai, Haidian and Changping portals for the OSS "innovation funds" mentioned in 2025.
